Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-integers]]) with $b > 0$. Then there exist
integers $q$ and $r$ with

$$a \;=\; qb + r, \qquad 0 \le r < b,$$

and the pair $(q,r)$ with these two properties is unique.

We say $b$ **divides** $a$, written $b \mid a$, when $a = qb$ for some
$q \in \mathbb{Z}$; by the above, for $b > 0$ this holds exactly when the
remainder $r$ is $0$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $b > 0$. Define $\Phi : \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ by

$$\Phi(u,v) \;=\; \begin{cases} (v,\; u - qv) & \text{if } v > 0, \\ (u,v) & \text{if } v \le 0, \end{cases}$$

where in the first clause $q$ is the unique quotient of $u$ by $v$ given by
[[thm-division-algorithm-in-z]], so that $u - qv$ is the remainder and
$0 \le u - qv < v$.

Let $R : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ be the unique function
with $R(0) = (a,b)$ and $R(\sigma(k)) = \Phi(R(k))$ supplied by the recursion
theorem ([[thm-recursion]]). Write $R(k) = (a_k, b_k)$; the sequence
$b_0, b_1, b_2, \dots$ is the **remainder descent** from $(a,b)$.

Then:

1. $b_k \ge 0$ for every $k$, and $b_{\sigma(k)} < b_k$ whenever $b_k > 0$;
2. $\gcd(a_k, b_k) = \gcd(a,b)$ for every $k$
   ([[def-common-divisor-and-gcd]]);
3. there is a least $N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $b_N = 0$, and $N \ne 0$; writing
   $N = \sigma(M)$, the value $b_M$ is the **last nonzero remainder**, and
   $b_M > 0$;
4. $a_N = b_M = \gcd(a,b)$.

So the descent terminates, and the last nonzero remainder is $\gcd(a,b)$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb Z$. Then $[a]_n$ is a unit of $\mathbb Z/n$
([[def-unit-group-modulo-n-and-euler-totient]]) if and only if

$$\gcd(a,n)=1,$$

that is, if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime ([[def-coprime]]). Consequently
the condition $\gcd(a,n)=1$ depends only on the class $[a]_n$.

Input an integer $n\ge2$ and the least residue $c\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Set $(r_{-1},r_0)=(n,c)$ and $(s_{-1},s_0)=(0,1)$. For $i=0,1,\ldots$, divide
$$
r_{i-1}=a_i r_i+r_{i+1},\qquad 0\le r_{i+1}<r_i,
$$
and update $s_{i+1}$ to the least residue of $s_{i-1}-a_i s_i$ modulo $n$. Stop at the first index $i$ for which $r_{i+1}=0$. Return the least residue $s_i$ if $r_i=1$, and return `NO_INVERSE` otherwise. For $c=0$, the first division has zero divisor under this indexing; handle it separately by returning `NO_INVERSE`.

The algorithm uses binary integer arithmetic. Its correctness and $O(B^3)$ bit bound for $B=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$ are proved in [[thm-qa-euclidean-modular-inverse-correctness-cost]].

derivations.claim: First handle $c=0$: since $n\ge2$, $\gcd(n,0)=n\ne1$, so the algorithm returns `NO_INVERSE`, correctly. Suppose $c>0$. The initialized coefficients satisfy $r_{-1}\equiv s_{-1}c\pmod n$ and $r_0=c\equiv s_0c\pmod n$.

If $r_{i-1}\equiv s_{i-1}c$ and $r_i\equiv s_i c$ modulo $n$, the division identity and update give
$$
r_{i+1}=r_{i-1}-a_i r_i\equiv(s_{i-1}-a_i s_i)c\equiv s_{i+1}c\pmod n.
$$
Replacing a coefficient by its least residue preserves this congruence. Induction proves $r_i\equiv s_i c\pmod n$ for every generated index.

By [F1], each positive remainder is strictly smaller than its predecessor, so the divisions terminate. By [F2], the last nonzero remainder is $d=\gcd(n,c)$. The algorithm returns an $s_i$ exactly when $d=1$; by [F3], this is exactly the unit case. If it returns, the invariant at the last nonzero index says $s_i c\equiv d=1\pmod n$, hence the returned least residue is an inverse. If $d\ne1$, [F3] says no inverse exists, so `NO_INVERSE` is correct.

Let $B=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$. There are $O(B)$ divisions: in two consecutive Euclidean divisions the remainder falls below half its earlier positive value. Indeed, if $r_{i+1}\le r_i/2$ this already holds; otherwise $r_{i+1}>r_i/2$, so the next quotient is $1$ and $r_{i+2}=r_i-r_{i+1}<r_i/2$. Thus at most two steps halve a positive remainder, which has at most $B$ bits.

Every quotient, remainder, and coefficient residue has $O(B)$ bits; each Euclidean quotient is found by binary long division in $O(B^2)$ bit operations. Each product $a_i s_i$ and reduction modulo $n$ also costs $O(B^2)$ by schoolbook multiplication and division. With $O(B)$ iterations from step 3.1, the total is $O(B^3)$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite projective measurement on $H$. Then $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$ lies in $[0,1]$ for every $a$, and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1$.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Write $\mathcal Q_n$ for the ordered tensor product of $n$ copies of the two-level register from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], with $\mathcal Q_0=\mathbb C$. Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$. Each $g\in G$ has an arity $r(g)\ge1$ and a specified unitary $U_g:\mathcal Q_{r(g)}\to\mathcal Q_{r(g)}$. An operation model states which listed gates may be called and what access or cost is assigned to them; the matrix $U_g$ by itself is only the mathematical gate data.

For $n\ge0$, the circuit wire set is $[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ in its displayed order and its state space is $\mathcal Q_n$. The computational basis word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})$ is assigned slot $\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$ from [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]], so wire $0$ is the most significant bit and the empty register has its single basis vector in slot $0$.

A gate occurrence on the $n$ wires is a pair $(g,(w_0,\ldots,w_{r(g)-1}))$ with distinct wire labels $w_j\in[n]$; the tuple order is the input and output factor order of the local gate. A layer is a finite ordered list of gate occurrences whose wire supports are pairwise disjoint. A unitary circuit is a finite chronological list $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ of such layers, with $L_1$ applied first and $L_d$ last; $d=0$ is the empty circuit. Its input, output, and terminally measured wires are specified as ordered lists without repetitions in $[n]$. This syntax specifies finite data only; the semantic action of gates on the full register is defined separately.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $E=(e_j)_{j<n}$ and $F=(f_i)_{i<m}$. Let $T:H\to K$ be
linear ([[def-linear-map]]), and write $T_{ij}$ for the $(i,j)$ entry of its
matrix in these bases.
Then, for every $z\in H$,

$$Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}f_i, \qquad T=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}|f_i\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

For $x\in K$ and $y\in H$, the rank-one map $|x\rangle\langle y|$ has
coordinate matrix $[x]_F[y]_E^\dagger$, where $M^\dagger=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$.
Its amplitude satisfies
$\langle x|T|y\rangle_D=\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}$.
All sums are empty when an index dimension is zero, and the identities include
those cases.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative with trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), define the outcome weight $p_a(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$. The **conditional state** for outcome $a$ is

$$\rho_a:=\begin{cases}\mathcal I_a(\rho)/p_a(\rho),&p_a(\rho)>0,\\[2pt]\bot,&p_a(\rho)=0.\end{cases}$$

Here $\bot$ is a symbol meaning that no conditional density operator is assigned; it is not a state. Positivity and normalization of the outcome weights, and density of every positive-probability conditional state, are proved in [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]].

Let $(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$, and let $M_a=E_a^{1/2}$ be the nonnegative square root of each effect. The maps

$$\mathcal I_a(X):=M_aXM_a,\qquad X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

form an instrument from $H$ to itself.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $\rho$ be a density operator and $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ a finite projective measurement on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$. If $p_a>0$, then

$$\rho_a:=\frac{P_a\rho P_a}{p_a}$$

is a density operator whose image $\operatorname{im}(\rho_a):=\{\rho_a x:x\in H\}$ is contained in $\operatorname{im}(P_a)$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). This statement assigns a conditional state only on positive-probability branches.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

derivations.claim: Put $\alpha=\exp(2\pi i ks/N)$ and $\beta=\exp(2\pi i\ell s/N)$. By [F8], $\alpha\beta=\exp(2\pi i(k+\ell)s/N)$. Expanding the input gives $\frac12(|00\rangle+\beta|01\rangle+\alpha|10\rangle+\alpha\beta|11\rangle)$. The map $C$ permutes the four orthonormal basis vectors by an involution, so it is unitary by [F2]. Its action sends this vector to $\frac12(|00\rangle+\beta|01\rangle+\alpha\beta|10\rangle+\alpha|11\rangle)$, in accordance with the ordered circuit semantics [F4].

The second-qubit-zero projection leaves $\frac12(|0\rangle+\alpha\beta|1\rangle)\otimes|0\rangle$. Its squared norm is $(1+|\alpha\beta|^2)/4=1/2$, since [F7] gives $|\alpha|=|\beta|=1$. By [F3], the pure-state density is the rank-one operator; [F5] gives its coordinate matrix and [F6] its trace, so the trace of the projected rank-one state is this squared norm. [F1] identifies it with the projective outcome weight. The Lüders conditional-state rule [F9] normalizes the joint branch; its product form and the partial trace [F10] leave first-qubit state $|\psi_{k+\ell}\rangle$.

The second-qubit-one projection leaves $\frac12(\beta|0\rangle+\alpha|1\rangle)\otimes|1\rangle$. Its squared norm is $(|\beta|^2+|\alpha|^2)/4=1/2$ by [F7]. As in step 2.1, [F3], [F5], and [F6] identify that squared norm with the trace weight, and [F1] gives the projective outcome probability. The Lüders conditional-state rule [F9] normalizes this joint branch; [F10] discards the measured second qubit. Since $\beta\ne0$, the normalized first-qubit vector is $\beta/|\beta|$ times $(|0\rangle+\alpha\overline\beta|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$; the factor is a global phase. By [F7] and [F8], $\alpha\overline\beta=\alpha\beta^{-1}=\exp(2\pi i(k-\ell)s/N)$. Thus the residual ray is $|\psi_{k-\ell}\rangle$. This calculation includes $k=\ell$ and either zero label.

Let $A$ be an abelian group, and let the cyclic group $C_2=\langle s\rangle$ ([[thm-classification-of-cyclic-groups]]) act on $A$ by inversion, $s\cdot a=a^{-1}$. The **generalized dihedral group** of $A$ is the external semidirect product ([[def-external-semidirect-product]])

$$\operatorname{Dih}(A)=A\rtimes C_2.$$

The inversion map is an automorphism precisely because $A$ is abelian.

Let $N$ and $H$ be groups ([[def-group]]), and let $\alpha:H\to\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ be an action by automorphisms ([[def-action-by-automorphisms]]). The **external semidirect product** $N\rtimes_\alpha H$ is the set $N\times H$ with multiplication

$$(n,h)(n',h')=\bigl(n\alpha_h(n'),hh'\bigr).$$

When the action is clear, the subscript is omitted.

Let $\alpha:H\to\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ be an action by automorphisms. The multiplication

$$(n,h)(n',h')=\bigl(n\alpha_h(n'),hh'\bigr)$$

makes $N\times H$ a group with identity $(1_N,1_H)$ and inverse

$$(n,h)^{-1}=\bigl(\alpha_{h^{-1}}(n^{-1}),h^{-1}\bigr).$$

Let $n,m\ge0$ and let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^m$ be a total Boolean function on ordered bit strings. Its coherent XOR oracle is the linear extension of
$$
O_f|x,y\rangle=|x,y\oplus f(x)\rangle
$$
on the ordered input and target computational basis, where XOR is componentwise. The declared access contract states how many invocations count as queries and whether a controlled invocation is supplied. A query to this declared black box is counted separately from elementary gate size, depth, and width.

If $f$ is supplied instead by an explicit Boolean circuit, implementing $O_f$ means compiling that circuit and paying its reversible elementary-gate and workspace costs; the function description alone is not a free query. For this XOR oracle, its inverse is the same map, as proved in [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Controlled access remains a separate capability unless the contract explicitly provides it.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For an integer $N\ge1$, let $\mathcal F_N$ be the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalized transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]. Define the **cyclic quantum Fourier transform** by $\operatorname{QFT}_N:=\mathcal F_N^{-1}$. The inverse exists by [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]], and its matrix on the standard basis indexed by $0,\ldots,N-1$ is

$$\operatorname{QFT}_N|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ixy/N}|y\rangle,\qquad 0\le x<N.$$

Here the standard-basis ket convention is the one specified by [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. Thus the transform has the positive sign and the same $N^{-1/2}$ normalization as the inverse Fourier formula. At $N=1$ it is the identity on the one-dimensional register. In the binary specialization $N=2^n$, the circuit page writes each index in its unique base-two expansion.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite projective measurement on $H$. Then $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$ lies in $[0,1]$ for every $a$, and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $E=(e_j)_{j<n}$ and $F=(f_i)_{i<m}$. Let $T:H\to K$ be
linear ([[def-linear-map]]), and write $T_{ij}$ for the $(i,j)$ entry of its
matrix in these bases.
Then, for every $z\in H$,

$$Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}f_i, \qquad T=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}|f_i\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

For $x\in K$ and $y\in H$, the rank-one map $|x\rangle\langle y|$ has
coordinate matrix $[x]_F[y]_E^\dagger$, where $M^\dagger=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$.
Its amplitude satisfies
$\langle x|T|y\rangle_D=\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}$.
All sums are empty when an index dimension is zero, and the identities include
those cases.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative with trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), define the outcome weight $p_a(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$. The **conditional state** for outcome $a$ is

$$\rho_a:=\begin{cases}\mathcal I_a(\rho)/p_a(\rho),&p_a(\rho)>0,\\[2pt]\bot,&p_a(\rho)=0.\end{cases}$$

Here $\bot$ is a symbol meaning that no conditional density operator is assigned; it is not a state. Positivity and normalization of the outcome weights, and density of every positive-probability conditional state, are proved in [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]].

Let $(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$, and let $M_a=E_a^{1/2}$ be the nonnegative square root of each effect. The maps

$$\mathcal I_a(X):=M_aXM_a,\qquad X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

form an instrument from $H$ to itself.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $\rho$ be a density operator and $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ a finite projective measurement on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$. If $p_a>0$, then

$$\rho_a:=\frac{P_a\rho P_a}{p_a}$$

is a density operator whose image $\operatorname{im}(\rho_a):=\{\rho_a x:x\in H\}$ is contained in $\operatorname{im}(P_a)$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). This statement assigns a conditional state only on positive-probability branches.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $(s,1)^2=(s-s,0)=(0,0)$, so $H_s$ has the two displayed elements. Right multiplication gives $(a,0)(s,1)=(a+s,1)$ and $(a,1)(s,1)=(a-s,0)$. Hence the distinct left cosets are $C_a=\{(a,0),(a+s,1)\}$ for $a\in A$: every group element occurs in one such pair, and the first coordinate of its unique $(\,\cdot\,,0)$ representative identifies the pair.

The initial state has amplitude $(2N)^{-1/2}$ on each group basis vector. After the oracle call in the declared circuit order [F8], the output basis label is constant on each $C_a$ and distinct for different $a$. By [F2]–[F4], tracing out the output retains exactly pairs of group labels in the same $C_a$, so the group-register operator is $\rho=\frac1{2N}\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{z,z'\in C_a}|z\rangle\langle z'|=\frac1N\sum_{a\in A}|C_a\rangle\langle C_a|$, where $|C_a\rangle=(|a,0\rangle+|a+s,1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Each $|C_a\rangle$ is normalized because its two distinct group basis vectors are orthonormal. The rank-one notation is the operator of [F7], with coordinate matrix and trace given by [F9]–[F10].

Applying [F5] to the first coordinate sends each coset vector to $$ |\phi'_a\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\exp(2\pi iak/N)|k\rangle\otimes|\psi_k\rangle. $$ The factorization uses [F12]. Let $\rho'=\frac1N\sum_a|\phi'_a\rangle\langle\phi'_a|$ be the transformed mixture from step 2.1. Under the Lüders branch [F13], $$ \Pi_k\rho'\Pi_k=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{a\in A}|k\rangle\langle k|\otimes|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|=\frac1N|k\rangle\langle k|\otimes|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|. $$ Its trace is $1/N$ by [F9]–[F11], so every $k$ occurs with that probability. The normalized conditional state on the joint register is $|k\rangle\langle k|\otimes|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|$. Discarding the first coordinate contracts its matching basis index by [F3]; after reordering the factors if needed by [F4], the retained qubit density is $|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|$. Hence the conditional qubit ray is $|\psi_k\rangle$, as claimed.

Let $A$ be an abelian group, and let the cyclic group $C_2=\langle s\rangle$ ([[thm-classification-of-cyclic-groups]]) act on $A$ by inversion, $s\cdot a=a^{-1}$. The **generalized dihedral group** of $A$ is the external semidirect product ([[def-external-semidirect-product]])

$$\operatorname{Dih}(A)=A\rtimes C_2.$$

The inversion map is an automorphism precisely because $A$ is abelian.

Let $N$ and $H$ be groups ([[def-group]]), and let $\alpha:H\to\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ be an action by automorphisms ([[def-action-by-automorphisms]]). The **external semidirect product** $N\rtimes_\alpha H$ is the set $N\times H$ with multiplication

$$(n,h)(n',h')=\bigl(n\alpha_h(n'),hh'\bigr).$$

When the action is clear, the subscript is omitted.

Let $\alpha:H\to\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ be an action by automorphisms. The multiplication

$$(n,h)(n',h')=\bigl(n\alpha_h(n'),hh'\bigr)$$

makes $N\times H$ a group with identity $(1_N,1_H)$ and inverse

$$(n,h)^{-1}=\bigl(\alpha_{h^{-1}}(n^{-1}),h^{-1}\bigr).$$

The input group is a finite abelian group $A$ supplied in explicit invariant-factor coordinates $A=\mathbb Z/n_1\mathbb Z\times\cdots\times\mathbb Z/n_d\mathbb Z$, with componentwise addition and the empty product allowed. The finite set $S$ is supplied with an injective fixed-length bit encoding. The input functions $f,g:A\to S$ are injective and have coherent XOR oracles with explicitly declared access and costs.

The promise is that there is a unique $s\in A$ such that
$$
f(a)=g(a+s)\qquad\text{for every }a\in A.
$$
The output is the coordinate encoding of $s$. The definition makes no claim that a group presented only by black-box operations comes with invariant-factor coordinates, efficient uniform preparations, efficient group operations, or an efficient implementation of either oracle.

Let $n,m\ge0$ and let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^m$ be a total Boolean function on ordered bit strings. Its coherent XOR oracle is the linear extension of
$$
O_f|x,y\rangle=|x,y\oplus f(x)\rangle
$$
on the ordered input and target computational basis, where XOR is componentwise. The declared access contract states how many invocations count as queries and whether a controlled invocation is supplied. A query to this declared black box is counted separately from elementary gate size, depth, and width.

If $f$ is supplied instead by an explicit Boolean circuit, implementing $O_f$ means compiling that circuit and paying its reversible elementary-gate and workspace costs; the function description alone is not a free query. For this XOR oracle, its inverse is the same map, as proved in [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Controlled access remains a separate capability unless the contract explicitly provides it.

In the ordered two-qubit basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the controlled-NOT with first wire control and second wire target is

$$\operatorname{CNOT}_{1\to2}|a,t\rangle=|a,t\mathbin{\oplus}a\rangle,\qquad a,t\in\{0,1\}.$$

Equivalently, it is the control block $C(X)=\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]], where $X$ is the Pauli bit-flip matrix. The wire order is part of the definition.

All bits are in $\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}$, with addition denoted by $\oplus$ and multiplication by juxtaposition. On three distinct ordered computational-basis wires, define the Toffoli gate $T$ and Fredkin gate $F$ by
$$
T|a,b,t\rangle=|a,b,t\oplus ab\rangle,
$$
and
$$
F|0,a,b\rangle=|0,a,b\rangle,\qquad F|1,a,b\rangle=|1,b,a\rangle.
$$
These basis actions extend linearly. Wire order is exactly the order displayed; the first two wires of $T$ are controls and the third is its target, while the first wire of $F$ is its control and the other two are conditionally swapped. Negative-control variants mean conjugating the chosen positive control by $X$ before and after the gate. These are fixed arity-three labels in the declared finite gate alphabet, not implicit access to arbitrary multicontrol gates. Their reversibility is established in [[lem-qc-x-cnot-toffoli-and-fredkin-are-involutions]].

derivations.claim:
By [F1], $(s,1)^2=(s-s,0)=(0,0)$, and $(s,1)\ne(0,0)$ because its second coordinate is $1$. Thus $H_s$ has the two stated elements. Right multiplication gives
$$
(a,0)(s,1)=(a+s,1),\qquad (a+s,1)(s,1)=(a,0).
$$
Consequently the left coset through $(a,0)$ is exactly $C_a=\{(a,0),(a+s,1)\}$. Every group element belongs to one such pair, and distinct $a$ give distinct pairs because their parity-zero representatives differ.

On the pair $C_a$, [F2] gives $F(a,0)=f(a)=g(a+s)=F(a+s,1)$. If two parity-zero values agree, injectivity of $f$ makes their coordinates equal; if two parity-one values agree, injectivity of $g$ does the same. If $F(a,0)=F(b,1)$, then $f(a)=g(b)=g(a+s)$, so injectivity of $g$ yields $b=a+s$ and the two inputs lie in $C_a$. Thus equality of $F$-values occurs exactly within one left coset.
The nonidentity element of $H_s$ is $(s,1)$, so equality $H_s=H_t$ forces $(s,1)=(t,1)$ and hence $s=t$.

A direct $F$-XOR oracle is exactly one value-query interface for the function just defined. Given only $O_f,O_g$, compute $f(a)$ and $g(a)$ into two fresh zero scratch registers with one call to each oracle. For each output bit, the selected value is $(1-b)f(a)_i\oplus b g(a)_i$; CNOT and Toffoli gates from [F4] implement this reversible Boolean-controlled XOR into the target, leaving the input and scratch registers unchanged. Apply $O_g$ and then $O_f$ again to erase the scratch registers, since [F3] makes each XOR oracle self-inverse and the group input is unchanged. The target has acquired precisely $F(a,b)$ and all scratch bits return to zero, using four calls total. This gives an explicit query account without postulating controlled access to $O_f$ or $O_g$.

A finite cyclic discrete-logarithm instance consists of a cyclic group $G=\langle g\rangle$ of known exact order $q\ge2$ and an element $x\in G$. Its answer is the unique integer $a\in\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$ satisfying $g^a=x$. Uniqueness follows because $g^u=g^v$ exactly when $u\equiv v\pmod q$.

For a quantum or bit-cost claim, the instance additionally declares an injective fixed-length encoding $\operatorname{enc}:G\to\{0,1\}^w$, with $w\ge\lceil\log_2q\rceil$, and one of the following operation profiles:

1. explicit reversible circuits for multiplication, equality, and any controlled multiplication used by the algorithm, with gate and clean-work costs; or
2. named group-operation oracles with a separate query charge for each operation. A controlled call is available only if that controlled operation is explicitly supplied and charged.

The associated hidden-subgroup function is $f:\mathbb Z_q\times\mathbb Z_q\to G$, $f(u,v)=g^u x^v$. A direct coherent XOR oracle for its fixed-length encoding is a separate supplied interface; if it is supplied, one call costs one $f$ query. Group-operation oracles do not automatically supply this function oracle, a controlled call, an inverse call, a gate implementation, or a classical bit-cost bound. No efficient implementation is asserted for every abstract finite cyclic group.

Inputs are integers $n,m\ge0$, $n$ distinct ordered Boolean input wires, an $m$-bit target register $y$ disjoint from the input wires, and a finite Boolean DAG with an explicit topological order and an ordered list of exactly $m$ output ports. Every vertex has a unique identifier; each non-input node is a constant $0$ or $1$, a NOT node of fan-in one, or an AND or OR node of fan-in two. Each source reference must name an input vertex or an earlier node in the supplied order. Each output port may name any input or non-input node, and repeated output ports are allowed. The Boolean graph uses the NOT/AND/OR basis with constants from [[def-boolean-circuit-size-depth-fanin-and-basis]], extended here to multiple ordered output ports sharing one graph.

Return INVALID if the input wires or graph vertices do not have distinct identifiers, a target wire overlaps an input or graph vertex, an unsupported gate or incorrect fan-in occurs, a source reference is unavailable at that position, the supplied order is invalid, or an output port names no available vertex. Otherwise:

1. Allocate one fresh clean value bit $w_v$ for each non-input node $v$.
2. Process nodes in the supplied order. Leave a constant-$0$ bit untouched; apply $X$ to a constant-$1$ bit. For a NOT node with input wire $u$, apply $X(w_v)$ then $\operatorname{CNOT}_{u\to w_v}$. For an AND node with inputs $u,v$, apply $T(u,v,w_v)$. For an OR node, apply $\operatorname{CNOT}_{u\to w_v}$, then $\operatorname{CNOT}_{v\to w_v}$, then $T(u,v,w_v)$. If a two-port node uses the same source identifier twice, first allocate a fresh clean scratch bit $s$, copy the source into $s$ by CNOT, use the distinct physical wires as the gate inputs, and uncopy $s$ immediately after writing $w_v$.
3. For each output port $j$, apply CNOT from its named input or value wire to target bit $y_j$.
4. Append the inverse of the entire node-evaluation list in reverse chronological order, including the temporary source-copy and uncopy instructions. Return the resulting finite gate list, with the input register unchanged and the target changed only by the stated XOR into $y$.

The inverse-list operation is defined instruction by instruction: $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli are each replaced by themselves, in reverse order. The Boolean graph is an explicit finite input; this procedure makes no uniform-generation, oracle, or Turing-time claim.

Let $n,m\ge0$, $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, and $y\in\{0,1\}^m$. Let a finite topologically ordered Boolean DAG have $S$ non-input nodes, including constants, and $E$ input-port uses counted with multiplicity. Its gates are NOT, AND, OR, and constants, with fan-in at most two, and it has $m$ ordered output ports computing $f(x)$. Under the fixed elementary alphabet in [[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]], counting each occurrence of $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli as one gate and one serial layer, [[alg-qc-reversible-embedding]] returns a circuit on the ordered input, target, and work registers implementing
$$
|x,y,0^w\rangle\longmapsto|x,y\oplus f(x),0^w\rangle
$$
for every basis input $x$ and every target string $y$. It uses at most $6S+4E+m$ elementary gate occurrences, at most $S+E$ clean work bits, and serial depth at most $6S+4E+m$. The same operator action holds coherently on arbitrary superpositions and after adjoining any finite reference register.

In the ordered two-qubit basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the controlled-NOT with first wire control and second wire target is

$$\operatorname{CNOT}_{1\to2}|a,t\rangle=|a,t\mathbin{\oplus}a\rangle,\qquad a,t\in\{0,1\}.$$

Equivalently, it is the control block $C(X)=\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]], where $X$ is the Pauli bit-flip matrix. The wire order is part of the definition.

Let $D$ be a finite ordered quantum register and let $A$ be an ordered register of $k\ge0$ ancilla qubits, with Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_D$ and $\mathcal H_A$. Write $|0_A\rangle=|0^k\rangle$, including $|0_A\rangle=1$ when $k=0$. Let $U$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$ and let $V$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D$.

The register $A$ is a **clean ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when
$$
U(|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle
$$
for every vector $|\psi\rangle_D$. Thus the data operation is independent of the input vector and all clean wires return exactly to zero.

The register $A$ is a **dirty ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when the operator identity $U=V\otimes I_A$ holds on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$. Equivalently, every product input $|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$ is mapped to $V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$, with the same $V$ for every data and ancilla vector. This requires exact restoration of an arbitrary, initially unknown ancilla state and forbids residual data–ancilla correlation.

These are exact contracts for the complete subroutine. A temporary intermediate alteration of an ancilla is permitted if the full unitary satisfies the stated identity.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

derivations.claim: For a valid code $z=\operatorname{enc}(u)$, the inverse property gives $h_{c^{-1}}(1,h_c(1,z))=z$ and $h_c(1,h_{c^{-1}}(1,z))=z$; for invalid $z$ both maps fix $z$, and for $b=0$ both fix $z$. Thus, for each fixed control $b$, the two supplied maps on the $w$-bit data register are inverse permutations on every data word, and the complete controlled map preserves $b$.
Apply [F2] to $h_c$ and $h_{c^{-1}}$ with separate fresh $w$-bit targets. By [F3], each XOR computation returns its internal work to zero and has at most $6S+4E+w$ gates and $S+E$ work bits.

Starting from control $b$, data code $z$, and a fresh target $t=0^w$, compute $h_c(b,z)$ into $t$. Swap $z$ and $t$ bitwise using three CNOTs per bit; on each pair $(u,v)$ the sequence $(u,v)\mapsto(u,u\oplus v)\mapsto(v,u\oplus v)\mapsto(v,u)$, so it swaps the registers. The accumulator now contains $h_c(b,z)$ and $t$ contains the old $z$.

Compute $h_{c^{-1}}(b,h_c(b,z))$ into the old-$z$ target by XOR. By step 1.1 this XORs $z$ with itself and clears $t$ to $0^w$. The inverse computation also restores its internal work to zero by [F3]. The resulting data is $h_c(b,z)$, with every work and temporary target bit zero, which is the clean-ancilla identity of [F5].

The forward and inverse embeddings use at most $12S+8E+2w$ gates in total; the three-CNOT swaps use $3w$ more. The two Boolean embeddings use at most $2(S+E)$ clean internal work bits and the swapped $w$-bit target is also clean on return. Hence the total bounds are $12S+8E+5w$ gates and $2(S+E)+w$ clean work wires.

2. named group-operation oracles with a separate query charge for each operation. A controlled call is available only if that controlled operation is explicitly supplied and charged.

The associated hidden-subgroup function is $f:\mathbb Z_q\times\mathbb Z_q\to G$, $f(u,v)=g^u x^v$. A direct coherent XOR oracle for its fixed-length encoding is a separate supplied interface; if it is supplied, one call costs one $f$ query. Group-operation oracles do not automatically supply this function oracle, a controlled call, an inverse call, a gate implementation, or a classical bit-cost bound. No efficient implementation is asserted for every abstract finite cyclic group.

An input group is given in explicit invariant-factor coordinates
$$G=\prod_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z,\qquad 2\le n_1\mid n_2\mid\cdots\mid n_r,$$
with componentwise addition and $N:=|G|=\prod_i n_i$. The empty product has $G=\{0\}$ and $N=1$. No procedure for finding these coordinates from a black-box group is included. A character label is a tuple $\mathbf k=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$, representing
$$\chi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf g):=\prod_{i=1}^r\exp(2\pi i k_i g_i/n_i).$$
The cyclic-character and product-character suppliers identify these labels with all of $\widehat G$.

The hiding input is a finite set $S$, an injective encoding $\eta:S\to\{0,1\}^m$, and a total function $F:G\to S$ for which there is an unknown subgroup $H\le G$ such that
$$F(\mathbf g)=F(\mathbf g')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbf g-\mathbf g'\in H.$$
This is the hiding promise. Put $b_i:=\lceil\log_2 n_i\rceil$ and $b:=\sum_i b_i$. Encode $g_i\in\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$ by the $b_i$-bit big-endian binary word of its least residue in $\{0,\ldots,n_i-1\}$, and encode $\mathbf g$ by concatenating these words in coordinate order; denote this injective code by $\operatorname{code}_G(\mathbf g)$. This uses the first-wire-most-significant-bit convention of [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]. Use the same coordinate widths and convention to encode character labels $\mathbf k$ as $\operatorname{code}_{\widehat G}(\mathbf k)$.

The hiding input also supplies a total Boolean function $\widetilde F:\{0,1\}^b\to\{0,1\}^m$ agreeing with $\eta\circ F$ on valid group codes; its values on invalid bit strings are part of the declared extension. The coherent XOR oracle acts by
$$O_{\widetilde F}|x,y\rangle=|x,y\oplus\widetilde F(x)\rangle$$
on all ordered input and target bit-string basis states. In particular, on valid codes it adds $\eta(F(\mathbf g))$ to the target. A named oracle call is charged as one query; a Boolean-circuit implementation is charged for its reversible gates. The model makes no claim that an arbitrary function has an efficient circuit.

The recovery algorithm outputs a finite list of character labels $\mathbf k^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf k^{(M)}$. It denotes the constraint set
$$K:=\{\mathbf g\in G:\chi_{\mathbf k^{(j)}}(\mathbf g)=1\text{ for every }1\le j\le M\}=\bigcap_{j=1}^M\ker\chi_{\mathbf k^{(j)}},$$
where $\ker\chi:=\{\mathbf g:\chi(\mathbf g)=1\}$ and the empty intersection is defined to be $G$. Success means $K=H$. The output remains this implicit common-kernel presentation; converting it to subgroup generators is outside the definition.
